definition: Adversarial means involving or marked by conflict between opposing sides.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word adversarial. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know adversarial should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The debate between the two market analysts turned adversarial within minutes, each treating the other's numbers as a target to be shot down.
Two sides can be opposed on a question and still trade friendly notes; adversarial means the relationship itself is organized around the conflict.
Warring goes further than adversarial — the contest has burst its rules and turned into open battle.

Oppositional names simple resistance to whatever is put forward — one person, or one bloc, pushing back. Adversarial needs two sides organized against each other, with the conflict built into the arrangement: a courtroom, a debate, a red-team drill. A lone dissenter is oppositional; a structure that runs on opposition is adversarial.

Cutthroat means ruthless, win-at-any-cost competition — rules and fairness are the first casualties. An adversarial contest can be perfectly fair and rule-bound: the sides are set against each other by design, but both play inside the lines. Cutthroat tells you how dirty the fight is; adversarial tells you the fight is the structure.

Twice a year the bank pays one team of specialists to break into its own vaults — digitally, and by any trick short of a crime.
The defense team knows they are coming, never when.
Executives call the exercise adversarial testing, and they mean the word precisely: the two teams exist to oppose each other, and the bank's safety is built out of their conflict.
Adversarial is the exact word because it names a situation involving or marked by conflict between opposing sides — conflict as the arrangement itself, not a lapse in manners.
The specialists aren't angry, and nobody carries a grudge to lunch; the opposition is the design.
That structural sense is what separates adversarial from plain unfriendliness.
Reach for adversarial when conflict is the arrangement — legal systems, negotiations, red-team drills — rather than a mood someone woke up in.
The person across the table in such a process is your adversary, this unit's noun for the role.
If the sides merely disagree, opposed is enough; save adversarial for structures built out of opposition.

For ten years, two labs had clashed over why young songbirds get lost in city light, each certain the other's data were flawed.
Rather than trade another round of critical papers, the teams tried something unusual: a deliberately adversarial collaboration.
Under written rules agreed on in advance, each team designed experiments meant to break the other's theory, and both promised to publish whatever resulted.
The arrangement was built on conflict, but it was conflict with referees: shared data, predictions registered ahead of time, and a coin flip for author order.
Two years later the joint paper settled the question -- and both labs admitted the structured fight had done what a decade of polite disagreement could not.
